title: Jeremy Strong Wrote to Mark Zuckerberg. The Harder Conversation Is With the Audience
dek: Jeremy Strong says he contacted Mark Zuckerberg before playing him in The Social Reckoning. His promise to approach the role with respect raises a sharper question: what does accuracy owe a living, powerful subject?
content:
## The message was not a request for permission

Jeremy Strong says he wrote directly to Mark Zuckerberg after taking the role of the Meta founder in *The Social Reckoning*, Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to *The Social Network*. According to reports published on August 12, Strong told Zuckerberg that he regarded the part and its factual accuracy as serious responsibilities. Strong said Zuckerberg replied, but he did not disclose what the response contained.

That distinction matters. Contacting a living subject can be research, courtesy or a way of testing one’s assumptions; it does not make the subject an editor. Strong’s public description suggests he wanted Zuckerberg to know that the performance would not begin from ridicule. It does not suggest that the actor sought approval for the finished portrait.

The exchange is news because the role arrives with two shadows. Jesse Eisenberg’s Zuckerberg in the 2010 film remains one of the most recognizable screen portraits of a technology executive. The real Zuckerberg, meanwhile, has become a more visible political and corporate figure than he was when that film was made. Strong is therefore not simply replacing an actor. He is stepping between an established fictional character and a living person whose public meaning has continued to change.

## Respect is a method, not a verdict

Strong’s choice of the word respect can sound like sympathy if it is detached from the work of acting. In practice, respect can mean refusing the easiest shortcut. A performer who begins by deciding that a subject is ridiculous will collect gestures that prove the decision: the haircut, the pauses, the practiced congressional answers. A performer who treats the subject as coherent has to ask what the person believes he is protecting and why his own choices make sense to him.

That does not absolve the subject. It creates a more demanding form of criticism. Power is most revealing when it is shown as a system of reasons rather than a costume worn by a villain. Strong has previously argued that portraying a controversial person as fully human is not the same as endorsing him. His work as Roy Cohn in *The Apprentice* depended on that separation.

For Zuckerberg, the challenge is especially sharp because audiences already know the mannerisms. An imitation can earn instant recognition while concealing the absence of a point of view. Strong reportedly studied extensive footage, including congressional testimony and Zuckerberg’s public Facebook history. The useful result of that preparation will not be a perfect vocal match. It will be whether the performance can show a mind adapting its language as scrutiny closes in.

## A sequel cannot pretend the first portrait disappeared

*The Social Reckoning* is described by Sony as a follow-up rather than a conventional continuation. Sorkin wrote the earlier film and now directs as well as writes the new one, but David Fincher is not returning and Eisenberg declined to reprise the role. Reports say the new story centers on the Facebook Files disclosures, with Mikey Madison playing whistleblower Frances Haugen and Jeremy Allen White playing journalist Jeff Horwitz.

Changing actors makes historical sense: the new film addresses a later era of Facebook and a different public Zuckerberg. It also creates an unavoidable comparison. Eisenberg’s performance established a clipped, wounded, competitive figure whose emotional logic belonged to Sorkin’s drama as much as to biography. Strong must make viewers recognize the same name without merely aging that construction.

The actor’s contact with Zuckerberg quietly acknowledges the problem. The sequel cannot build only on another actor’s interpretation, because the person outside the film has supplied sixteen more years of testimony, product launches, political accommodations and public reinvention. Research becomes a way to break the inherited character open.

## Accuracy has limits in a film about disputed power

Strong’s reference to veracity should not be confused with documentary proof. A dramatic film compresses time, combines conversations and creates private scenes that no public record can fully verify. *The Social Network* was widely admired without being accepted as a literal account of every motive or exchange, and Zuckerberg publicly criticized parts of its portrayal.

The new film faces an even more contested record. The Facebook Files reporting concerns internal documents, platform decisions and competing claims about harm, responsibility and knowledge. A performance can be exact about posture and speech while the screenplay’s selection of events determines the argument. Accuracy therefore lives at several levels: what happened, what executives knew, what they said publicly and what the film imagines they believed privately.

Strong can take responsibility for the last of those only through performance. He cannot make the screenplay neutral, and neutrality would be a false promise in any case. What he can do is resist telling the audience how to feel before the scene has made its evidence visible.

## The real test is whether the performance leaves room to judge

A satirical Zuckerberg would be easy to market. A saintly one would be impossible to defend. The harder performance is one that allows intelligence, calculation, conviction and harm to occupy the same frame. That is where Strong’s message becomes more than an actor’s unusual piece of preparation. It states a boundary between taking a person seriously and accepting that person’s account of himself.

The reports leave important facts unresolved. Zuckerberg’s reply remains private, and there is no indication that he participated further or influenced the production. Audiences should not treat the contact as validation from the film’s subject. Nor should they assume it compromised the portrait before seeing it.

*The Social Reckoning* is scheduled for theatrical release on October 9. By then, the publicity campaign will probably turn Strong’s physical transformation into the most convenient image. The more consequential transformation will be harder to capture in a trailer: whether he can replace a famous movie character with a person recognizable enough to be judged anew.

Writing to Zuckerberg may have been respectful. The film’s obligation is different. It has to respect the audience enough to show power without simplifying it.
